opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core issue is that human feedback works really well when the person giving the feedback can actually tell which answer is better. Early on, when models were making obvious mistakes, like getting a fact wrong, being rude, going off-topic, almost anyone could look at two responses and say, "this one's better." That's what made RLHF so effective in the first place.

But as models get more capable, the tasks they're doing start to exceed what a typical rater can evaluate quickly. If a model writes a few hundred lines of code, or a subtle legal argument, or a proof in some niche area of math, you'd need a real expert, and even then they might need hours to check it carefully. So you get this situation where the labels get noisier, more expensive, and slower, right at the point where you most need them to be precise.

And there's a subtler failure mode too. When people can't fully verify the substance, they fall back on surface features: does it sound confident, is it well formatted, does it agree with what I already believed? So you can end up training the model to be persuasive rather than correct, or to be sycophantic, telling people what they want to hear. That's actively dangerous as capabilities go up, because a very capable model optimized that way gets really good at looking right.

That's a big part of why we've invested in approaches like Constitutional AI and, more broadly, scalable oversight. The idea is to use the AI itself to help with evaluation: have models critique each other, break hard problems into pieces humans *can* check, and write down principles explicitly so the training signal comes from something more legible than a thumbs up or thumbs down. Humans stay in the loop, but they're supervising the process and the principles rather than trying to personally grade every single output. I think figuring that out well is one of the most important problems in the field right now.

r001.rationale: The response explains that increasingly complex outputs exceed a typical rater’s ability to evaluate and may require a real expert hours to check, making qualified judgment harder.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core issue is that human feedback only works when the human can actually tell the difference between a good answer and a great one. In the early days that was easy. The model would say something obviously wrong, or rambling, or off-topic, and anyone could point at it and say, "no, this one's better." But as the models get stronger, the gap between two outputs gets subtler and subtler, and eventually the model is operating in territory where the human rater just isn't qualified to judge.

Think about asking a model to write a thousand lines of code, or review a proof, or summarize a dense legal document. A rater has maybe a few minutes per example. They're going to grade on surface features: does it look confident, is it well-formatted, is it the right length. And the model learns those surface features really efficiently. So you end up optimizing for "seems good to a tired human skimming it" rather than "is actually correct." That's sycophancy, that's verbosity, that's confidently stated nonsense. The feedback signal gets noisier right as you need it to be sharpest.

There's also a ceiling problem. If you're learning from humans ranking outputs, you're bounded by what humans can recognize as good. You can't easily train a model to be better than your raters at a task using that method alone, because the signal literally comes from the raters. So the whole paradigm starts to run out of room.

That's a big part of why we've moved toward things like Constitutional AI and AI feedback, where you write down principles and have the model critique and revise itself against them, and toward areas where you have verifiable outcomes, like code that either passes tests or doesn't, or math where you can check the answer. The human role shifts from grading every output to specifying what we want at a higher level and auditing the process. Which I actually think is the right place for humans to be. We're much better at saying "here's what good looks like" than at reliably spotting it a thousand times a day.

r001.rationale: The response says that as models improve, they operate in areas where human raters may not be qualified to judge outputs, and illustrates this with complex code, proofs, and legal documents.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental issue is that giving good feedback requires you to understand whether the model did a good job. And as models become more capable, they can produce things that are harder for a human to evaluate. If a model writes a thousand lines of code, you might need an expert to spend hours figuring out whether it’s actually correct.

That creates a gap between what looks good to the person giving feedback and what actually is good. A clear, confident answer is easy to reward. A subtle mistake in the reasoning is much harder to catch. So you can end up training models to be persuasive rather than correct, even without intending to.

The interesting question is how you scale oversight along with capability. Can you use models to help humans check the work? Can you break a hard problem into pieces that are easier to verify? Human feedback is still valuable, but you need more than someone looking at two answers and picking the one they like better.

r001.rationale: The response says capable models produce outputs that are harder to evaluate and may require an expert to review them for hours. It does not explain that finding people with sufficient expertise to judge those outputs becomes more difficult.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the fundamental issue is that it gets harder for a human to tell whether the model did a good job. If you ask it a simple question, you can evaluate the answer pretty easily. But if you ask it to write a large piece of software or reason through a complicated scientific problem, giving good feedback might require hours of work—or expertise you don’t have.

And there’s a distinction between an answer that looks good and an answer that’s actually correct. Human feedback can reward something that’s convincing, even when it has a subtle flaw. As models become more capable, that gap becomes more important. So the challenge is: how do we provide reliable oversight when evaluating the work is itself a really difficult task?

r001.rationale: The response says judging complex outputs may require expertise the evaluator lacks, making reliable human oversight harder as models become more capable.
